claim: In an MIT Election Lab illustration, the same 100 voters, split 50-50 between two parties across four districts, can give a 2-2 seat split or a 3-1 win for either party, depending only on where the lines are drawn.
fact_check_evidence: MIT page: four 5x5 districts; compact plan gives 2-2; packing one party gives the other 3-1; the reverse gives 3-1 the other way, with each party holding 50 of the cells. Wikipedia's gerrymandering article shows an equivalent 50-voter grid example. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerrymandering https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/redistricting)

claim: Canada readjusts its federal electoral boundaries after every 10-year census to reflect changes in population.
fact_check_evidence: Elections Canada: readjustment after each decennial census in accordance with the Constitution Act, 1867 and the EBRA. Library of Parliament research publication describes the same cycle. (https://lop.parl.ca/sites/PublicWebsite/default/en_CA/ResearchPublications/202227E https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Boundaries_Readjustment_Act)

claim: Since the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act of 1964, independent commissions, one per province and each chaired by a judge, draw Canada's federal districts; sitting legislators cannot serve on them.
fact_check_evidence: Elections Canada: in 1964 Parliament gave the task to independent commissions, one per province; chairs are judges; members of the Senate, Commons or provincial legislatures are ineligible. House of Commons Procedure and Practice agrees. (https://www.ourcommons.ca/procedure/procedure-and-practice-4/ch04-3-e.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Boundaries_Readjustment_Act)

claim: The word gerrymander comes from 1812, when Massachusetts governor Elbridge Gerry signed a bill creating oddly shaped districts that helped his party; a Boston Gazette cartoon drew one as a salamander, the 'Gerry-mander'.
fact_check_evidence: Mass Moments: Gerry signed the 1812 bill; a district map drawn as a salamander was named the Gerry-mander and appeared as a cartoon in the Boston Gazette. Smithsonian Magazine and the Library of Congress date the cartoon to 26 March 1812. (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/where-did-term-gerrymander-come-180964118/ https://blogs.loc.gov/law/2017/02/elbridge-gerry-and-the-monstrous-gerrymander/)

claim: Gerrymandering is the deliberate drawing of electoral district boundaries to help or hurt a particular political interest.
fact_check_evidence: IDEA handbook glossary: deliberate manipulation of electoral district boundaries so as to advantage or disadvantage a particular political interest. MIT Election Lab: intentional manipulation of district boundaries. (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/redistricting https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/gerrymander)

claim: Packing crowds a group's voters into as few districts as possible; cracking spreads them thinly across many districts. Both leave that group with fewer seats.
fact_check_evidence: MIT: packing crowds voters into as few districts as possible so they win fewer seats; cracking spreads them across many districts to limit influence. Brennan Center's explainer gives the same definitions. (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/gerrymandering-explained https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerrymandering)

claim: Law professor Nicholas Stephanopoulos and researcher Eric McGhee (2015) proposed the efficiency gap, which compares each party's 'wasted' votes: votes for losers and votes beyond what a winner needed.
fact_check_evidence: Ballotpedia and Wikipedia: 2015 University of Chicago Law Review article defines the efficiency gap as the difference in wasted votes divided by total votes; wasted votes are those for losers and those beyond 50% for winners. (https://ballotpedia.org/Efficiency_gap https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efficiency_gap)

claim: Political scientists Jowei Chen and Jonathan Rodden (2013) found that when one party's voters are concentrated in cities, maps drawn without partisan intent can still give it fewer seats than its share of votes.
fact_check_evidence: Chen and Rodden, QJPS 2013 (Stanford preprint and Brennan Center copy): voters inefficiently concentrated in cities can expect fewer than 50% of seats with 50% of votes; bias emerges from human geography without intentional gerrymandering. (https://web.stanford.edu/~jrodden/wp/florida.pdf https://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/legal-work/Chen_Rodden_Through_the_Thicket_2015.pdf)

claim: In 1940, Paul Lazarsfeld and colleagues interviewed the same voters again and again in Erie County, Ohio, through a US presidential campaign; the study became the 1944 book The People's Choice.
fact_check_evidence: Encyclopedia.com: the Erie County (Ohio) study used panel surveys and led to The People's Choice (1944) by Lazarsfeld, Berelson and Gaudet. Springer and Columbia University Press confirm repeated monthly interviews during the 1940 campaign. (https://cup.columbia.edu/book/the-peoples-choice/9780231197953/ https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-531-90400-9_62)

claim: Contrary to their expectations, the researchers found radio and newspapers had only minor direct effects on how people voted; people mainly decided through conversations with those around them.
fact_check_evidence: Encyclopedia.com: contrary to expectations, radio and print had relatively minor direct effects; people decided mainly on the basis of interpersonal communication with peers. Elgar Encyclopedia (minimal effects theory) and Springer summaries agree. (https://www.elgaronline.com/display/book/9781035301447/vol2.chapter124.xml https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-658-50422-9_1)

claim: Lazarsfeld's two-step flow: ideas move from the media to opinion leaders, and then from them to their followers through personal networks.
fact_check_evidence: Encyclopedia.com: two-step flow, in which ideas move from the media to opinion leaders and then to their followers through interpersonal networks. Springer chapter on the two-step flow model describes the same. (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-658-50422-9_1 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-step_flow_of_communication)

claim: UK law limits how much each party may spend in the 365 days before a general election, with the limit rising with the number of seats it contests.
fact_check_evidence: Institute for Government: limits apply to the 365 days before polling day, calculated per constituency contested. Electoral Commission guidance on the party spending limit describes the same per-seat calculation. (https://www.electoralcommission.org.uk/party-spending-and-pre-poll-donations-and-loans-uk-parliamentary-general-election/spending-limit)

claim: In Buckley v. Valeo (1976), the US Supreme Court upheld limits on contributions to campaigns but struck down limits on campaign spending as restrictions on free expression.
fact_check_evidence: First Amendment Encyclopedia: contribution limits not a First Amendment violation, spending limits unconstitutional. Congressional Research Service (R43719) and Britannica summarise the 1976 ruling the same way. (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R43719 https://www.britannica.com/event/Buckley-v-Valeo)

claim: In 1936 the Literary Digest mailed about 10 million straw ballots, got 2.4 million back and predicted Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt; Roosevelt won easily.
fact_check_evidence: Emory math center: 10 million ballots sent, 2.4 million returned, Landon predicted 57-43; Roosevelt won 62-37. ProQuest and Wikipedia (The Literary Digest) give the same figures. (https://about.proquest.com/en/blog/2016/That-Time-the-Literary-Digest-Poll-Got-1936-Election-Wrong/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Literary_Digest)

claim: The Digest drew its sample from phone lists, car registrations and club memberships, which during the Depression leaned toward the well-off, and only about a quarter of those mailed replied.
fact_check_evidence: Emory: sample from phone numbers, driver registrations and country club memberships, more often available to the rich in the Depression; about 25% return rate. Squire (Social Science History) and Wikipedia stress the low response as well. (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/social-science-history/article/president-landon-and-the-1936-literary-digest-poll/E360C38884D77AA8D71555E7AB6B822C https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Literary_Digest)

claim: George Gallup, using more systematic, scientific sampling, publicly predicted in 1936 that Roosevelt would win re-election handily.
fact_check_evidence: Gallup: Dr. Gallup used systematic, scientific sampling and went public predicting Roosevelt would win handily. Wikipedia and ProQuest note Gallup correctly called the 1936 result with a far smaller sample. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Literary_Digest https://about.proquest.com/en/blog/2016/That-Time-the-Literary-Digest-Poll-Got-1936-Election-Wrong/)

claim: A margin of error of plus or minus 3 points at 95% confidence means that if the same survey were run 100 times, the result would be within 3 points of the true value about 95 times.
fact_check_evidence: Pew: fielded 100 times, within 3 points of the true value 95 of those times. AAPOR's margin of sampling error guide gives the same interpretation. (https://aapor.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/Margin-of-Sampling-Error-508.pdf)

claim: A simple random sample of 1,067 people has a margin of error of about plus or minus 3 percentage points for a candidate's overall support.
fact_check_evidence: Pew: a simple random sample of 1,067 cases has a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points. Pew's sample-size table and standard formula (1.96 x sqrt(0.25/1067) = 3.0%) agree. (https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Table-with-sample-sizes-and-margins-of-error.pdf)

claim: The margin of error on the gap between two candidates is roughly double: a 3-point margin for each becomes about 6 points for a lead, so a 5-point lead could really be anywhere from -1 to +11.
fact_check_evidence: Pew: the 3-point margin for each candidate becomes approximately a 6-point margin for the difference; a 5-point lead could be between -1 and +11. AAPOR guidance notes the margin for a difference is larger than for a single estimate. (https://aapor.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/Margin-of-Sampling-Error-508.pdf)

claim: Sampling error is only one of many possible sources of error in polls; question wording and who is less likely to be reached or respond also affect results.
fact_check_evidence: Pew: sampling variability is only one of many sources of error; question wording and respondents less likely to be sampled or respond matter. Undark's 2020 article on margin of error makes the same point. (https://undark.org/2020/11/23/polls-margin-of-error-gets-new-scrutiny/)

claim: A referendum gives people a direct vote, binding or advisory, on a specific issue referred to them by governing institutions such as a parliament or president.
fact_check_evidence: IDEA primer: referendums give the people a direct vote, binding or advisory, on a specific issue referred by governing institutions (presidents, cabinets, parliaments). IDEA's Direct Democracy Handbook overview uses the same definition. (https://www.idea.int/sites/default/files/publications/chapters/direct-democracy-the-international-idea-handbook/direct-democracy-the-international-idea-handbook-overview-EN.pdf https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum)

claim: A citizens' initiative is a direct vote started by the people themselves, typically through a petition signed by a set number of people.
fact_check_evidence: IDEA primer: citizens' initiatives are initiated by the people, typically proposed by a petition with a certain number of signatures. Wikipedia's popular initiative article agrees. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_initiative)

claim: In practice, advisory referendums are usually treated as politically binding, especially when the result is decisive.
fact_check_evidence: IDEA primer: advisory referendums are usually treated as politically, if not legally, binding, especially if the result is decisive. Wikipedia's referendum article notes non-binding votes often carry political weight. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum)

claim: In a binding referendum in 1993, 53.9% of New Zealand voters chose MMP over first-past-the-post.
fact_check_evidence: Search of Te Ara and Wikipedia: 1993 binding referendum, MMP supported by 53.9%, FPP 46.1%, leading to the Electoral Act 1993. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_New_Zealand_electoral_reform_referendum https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_reform_in_New_Zealand)

claim: In 1988, Chile's authoritarian ruler Augusto Pinochet unexpectedly lost a referendum to extend his term, and his regime collapsed shortly after.
fact_check_evidence: IDEA primer: in 1988 Pinochet unexpectedly lost a referendum to extend his term and his regime collapsed shortly thereafter. Wikipedia's 1988 Chilean national plebiscite article confirms the No side won, leading to open elections in 1989. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Chilean_national_plebiscite)

claim: Elliot Bulmer's International IDEA primer says referendums let citizens vote on a single measure on its own merits, instead of only choosing a party's whole package of policies.
fact_check_evidence: IDEA primer (Bulmer, 2nd ed. 2017): referendums let citizens separate out their preferences, voting on measures on their own merits, decoupled from manifestos. IDEA's catalogue page lists Bulmer as author. (https://www.idea.int/publications/catalogue/direct-democracy)

claim: Bulmer also lists criticisms: voters may be swayed by unrelated factors such as how popular party leaders are, frequent votes can cause voter fatigue, and rulers can use referendums to fake legitimacy.
fact_check_evidence: IDEA primer: voter irrationality (unrelated factors such as standing of party leaders), voter fatigue, and authoritarian abuse creating a false veneer of legitimacy. IDEA's Direct Democracy Handbook overview discusses the same risks. (https://www.idea.int/sites/default/files/publications/chapters/direct-democracy-the-international-idea-handbook/direct-democracy-the-international-idea-handbook-overview-EN.pdf)

claim: The Council of Europe's Venice Commission says a referendum question must be clear, must not be misleading and must not suggest an answer.
fact_check_evidence: Venice Commission Code of Good Practice on Referendums (2007) and its 2022 revision: question must be clear, not misleading, not suggest an answer. The Council of Europe opinion page and PACE report restate this. (https://www.coe.int/en/web/venice-commission/-/opinion-371 https://rm.coe.int/revised-code-of-good-practice-on-referendums-adopted-by-the-council-fo/1680a8115a)

claim: At UK elections, candidates can appoint counting agents to watch the verification and count, and the count is meant to be transparent.
fact_check_evidence: Electoral Commission: counting agents may be appointed to observe verification and counting; count processes should be transparent. Edinburgh's 2024 count guidance and Wikipedia's counting agent article agree. (https://www.edinburgh.gov.uk/documents/uk-parliament-election-2024-guidance-count-procedures-candidates-election-agents-counting-agents/9 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting_agent)

claim: At UK elections, candidates can appoint counting agents to watch the verification and count, and the count is meant to be transparent.
fact_check_evidence: Electoral Commission: counting agents may be appointed to observe verification and counting; count processes should be transparent. Edinburgh's 2024 count guidance and Wikipedia's counting agent article agree. (https://www.edinburgh.gov.uk/documents/uk-parliament-election-2024-guidance-count-procedures-candidates-election-agents-counting-agents/9 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting_agent)

claim: A candidate's agent may ask for a recount; the returning officer must consider it but may refuse an unreasonable request, and any recount happens in full view of those present.
fact_check_evidence: Electoral Commission: returning officer must consider any recount request but may refuse if unreasonable; recounts carried out in full view. Preston council's copy of the Commission's verification and count guidance says the same. (https://www.preston.gov.uk/media/22916/EC-Guidance-Verification-and-Count/pdf/7._Verification_and_Count_1.pdf?m=1756896424363)

claim: If candidates tie and one more vote would decide the result, the returning officer must decide between them by drawing lots.
fact_check_evidence: Electoral Commission: where an equality of votes exists and an added vote would elect a candidate, the returning officer decides by lot. The parliamentary election rules (Representation of the People Act 1983, Sch. 1 r. 49) provide the same. (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1983/2/schedule/1 https://erskinemay.parliament.uk/section/4926/procedure-under-the-representation-of-the-people-act-1983)

claim: In India, a VVPAT printer attached to each voting machine shows the voter a paper slip with the candidate's name and symbol for 7 seconds; it then drops into a sealed box, where the slips can be counted.
fact_check_evidence: CEO Manipur FAQ: slip with serial number, name and symbol visible through a window for 7 seconds, then falls into a sealed drop box; slips may be counted. Supreme Court Observer and Drishti describe the same 7-second slip. (https://www.scobserver.in/cases/vvpats-for-voter-verification-association-for-democratic-reforms-v-election-commission-of-india/ https://www.drishtiias.com/daily-updates/daily-news-analysis/voter-verified-paper-audit-trail-vvpat)

claim: Statistician Philip Stark developed risk-limiting audits in 2007: officials hand-check randomly chosen paper ballots, and if the sample doesn't confirm the result, the audit grows up to a full hand count, which replaces the reported result.
fact_check_evidence: Stark (2018): RLAs developed in 2007, first published 2008; a full manual tally replaces the reported result if triggered. US Election Assistance Commission and Rivest's ClipAudit paper describe RLAs as hand-checking random ballots and escalating. (https://www.eac.gov/sites/default/files/eac_assets/1/6/Risk-Limiting_Audits_-_Practical_Application_Jerome_Lovato.pdf https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.08312)

claim: Risk-limiting audits have been tested in California, Ohio and Denmark.
fact_check_evidence: Stark (2018) footnote: RLAs required in Colorado and Rhode Island and tested in California, Ohio and Denmark. Stark and Teague's paper on RLAs for D'Hondt discusses Danish application. (https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/jets15/jets_0301_stark.pdf)

claim: Stark compares ballot-polling audits to exit polls, noting that 'unlike voters, ballots have to reply, and have to reply truthfully.'
fact_check_evidence: Stark (2018) footnote 9 contains the quoted line verbatim; the same comparison appears in Lindeman and Stark's 'A Gentle Introduction to Risk-Limiting Audits'. (https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~stark/Preprints/lhc18.pdf)

claim: In a 2017 Council of Europe report, Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan separated misinformation (false, shared without meaning harm), disinformation (false, shared knowingly to cause harm) and malinformation (genuine, shared to cause harm).
fact_check_evidence: Council of Europe report (31 October 2017) by Wardle and Derakhshan defines the three types. EPRA's news item and Wikipedia's malinformation article give the same definitions. (https://www.epra.org/news_items/council-of-europe-s-report-identifies-strategies-to-tackle-disinformation https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malinformation)

claim: Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew watched 10 PhD historians, 10 professional fact checkers and 25 Stanford undergraduates judge live websites on social and political issues.
fact_check_evidence: ERIC abstract: 45 users, 10 historians, 10 fact checkers, 25 Stanford undergraduates, evaluating live websites on issues such as minimum wage. Stanford Report (2017) describes the same study. (https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2017/10/fact-checkers-outperform-historians-evaluating-online-information https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/016146811912101102)

claim: Historians and students often fell for official-looking logos and domain names, and read vertically, staying on a website to judge whether it was reliable.
fact_check_evidence: ERIC abstract: historians and students fell victim to official-looking logos and domain names and read vertically. Stanford Report: they stayed within the site and were taken in by professional-looking names and logos. (https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2017/10/fact-checkers-outperform-historians-evaluating-online-information)

claim: Fact checkers read laterally: after a quick scan they left the site and opened new tabs to see what others said about it, reaching better-founded conclusions in a fraction of the time.
fact_check_evidence: ERIC abstract: fact checkers read laterally, leaving a site after a quick scan and opening new tabs; more warranted conclusions in a fraction of the time. Stanford Report and the SSRN version agree. (https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2017/10/fact-checkers-outperform-historians-evaluating-online-information https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3048994)

claim: Mike Caulfield's SIFT method has four moves: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims, quotes and media back to the original context.
fact_check_evidence: Caulfield's Hapgood post lists the four moves. University library guides (UC Merced, UChicago, Princeton) attribute SIFT to Caulfield with the same four steps. (https://libguides.ucmerced.edu/news/evaluation/sift-method https://guides.lib.uchicago.edu/c.php?g=1241077&p=9082322)

claim: Caulfield's first move: when you first hit a page or post, stop and ask whether you know what the source is before reading or sharing it.
fact_check_evidence: Hapgood: when you first hit a page or post, STOP and ask whether you know the website or source. UC Merced's SIFT guide: don't read or share until you know what it is. (https://libguides.ucmerced.edu/news/evaluation/sift-method)

claim: Caulfield notes that much of what we find online has been stripped of context, like a video clip that leaves out what happened before.
fact_check_evidence: Hapgood: much of what we find on the internet has been stripped of context, e.g. a video of a fight without what happened before. Wayne State's SIFT guide on tracing to original context says the same. (https://guides.lib.wayne.edu/sift/find https://libguides.ucmerced.edu/news/evaluation/sift-method)

claim: On 26 March 1994 in Paris, the Inter-Parliamentary Council unanimously adopted the Inter-Parliamentary Union's Declaration on Criteria for Free and Fair Elections.
fact_check_evidence: IPU archive text header: unanimously adopted by the Inter-Parliamentary Council at its 154th session (Paris, 26 March 1994). ACE Project and the University of Minnesota Human Rights Library carry the same text. (https://aceproject.org/ero-en/topics/election-integrity/inter-parliamentary-union-declaration-on-criteria-for-free-and-fair-elections-1994 https://hrlibrary.umn.edu/monitoring/chapter14.html)

claim: The Declaration says a government's authority can only derive from the will of the people, expressed in genuine, free and fair elections held at regular intervals.
fact_check_evidence: IPU text section 1; the IPU's current Declaration page and ACE Project copy restate the principle with universal, equal and secret suffrage. (https://www.ipu.org/impact/democracy-and-strong-parliaments/ipu-standards/declaration-criteria-free-and-fair-elections https://aceproject.org/ero-en/topics/election-integrity/inter-parliamentary-union-declaration-on-criteria-for-free-and-fair-elections-1994)

claim: It says the right to vote in secret is absolute, every vote should carry equivalent weight, candidates should campaign on an equal basis, and states should ensure an honest count, with party agents and accredited observers present.
fact_check_evidence: IPU text: 2(7) right to vote in secret is absolute; 2(6) equivalent weight; 3(3) campaign on an equal basis; 4(2) integrity of the process for counting votes; 4(7) party agents and duly accredited observers. The ACE Project copy matches. (https://aceproject.org/ero-en/topics/election-integrity/inter-parliamentary-union-declaration-on-criteria-for-free-and-fair-elections-1994)

claim: In the Netherlands, private schools are exclusively or largely government-dependent.

claim: UK MPs are elected to represent the interests and concerns of all the people who live in their constituency, whether they voted for them or not.
appears_in: L93 card.government.093.c1; L96 card.government.096.c4; L98 card.government.098.c4
fact_check_evidence: The UK Parliament wording is reproduced on many MPs' own sites (e.g. Helen Whately, Robert Buckland): MPs represent all people in the constituency whether they voted for them or not. (https://www.helenwhately.org.uk/what-mp-and-what-can-they-do https://www.robertbuckland.co.uk/what-can-mp-do)

claim: UK MPs can normally only deal with issues raised by people who live in their constituency, called constituents.
fact_check_evidence: MPs' sites reproducing Parliament's guidance say MPs are only able to deal with issues raised by people who live in their constituency. (https://www.jeremywright.org.uk/what-can-mp-do https://www.carolinenokes.com/what-can-mp-do)

claim: Most UK MPs hold surgeries in their constituency, where people can meet them and discuss matters of concern.
fact_check_evidence: Parliament's glossary defines surgeries this way; MPs' sites describe holding advice surgeries for constituents. (https://www.helenwhately.org.uk/what-mp-and-what-can-they-do https://theconversation.com/explainer-what-does-a-british-mp-actually-do-41045)

claim: UK Parliament petitions that reach 10,000 signatures get a response from the government; those that reach 100,000 are considered for debate in Parliament.
fact_check_evidence: The petitions site help page states both thresholds; news explainers of the petitions system repeat them. (https://petition.parliament.uk/help https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petitions_Committee_(House_of_Commons))

claim: A Canadian House of Commons e-petition needs at least 500 signatures to be presented, and the government responds within 45 days of presentation.
fact_check_evidence: The House of Commons signatory guide and Procedure and Practice (ch. 22) give the 500-signature threshold and 45-day government response. (https://www.ourcommons.ca/petitions/en/Home/AboutContent?guide=PIGuideForSignatories https://www.ourcommons.ca/procedure-and-practice-4/ch22-1-e.html)

claim: The ILO defines volunteer work as unpaid, non-compulsory work: time people give without pay to activities done through an organization or directly for others outside their own household.

claim: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted by the General Assembly on 20 November 1989 and is the world's most widely ratified human rights treaty.
fact_check_evidence: UNICEF and OHCHR both give the 1989 adoption and describe the CRC as the most widely ratified human rights treaty. (https://www.unicef.org/child-rights-convention/convention-text https://www.ohchr.org/en/treaty-bodies/crc/background-convention)

claim: The Convention defines a child as every human being below the age of 18, unless the law applicable to the child sets adulthood earlier.
fact_check_evidence: Article 1 as published by UNICEF; the same text appears in the MUNUC copy of the Convention. (https://www.unicef.org/child-rights-convention/convention-text https://munuc.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/CRC.pdf)

claim: Article 12 of the Convention gives a child capable of forming views the right to express them freely in all matters affecting the child, given due weight according to age and maturity.
fact_check_evidence: Article 12(1) as published by UNICEF; UNICEF Australia's summary says children should be free to have opinions in all matters affecting them. (https://www.unicef.org/child-rights-convention/convention-text https://www.unicef.org.au/convention-rights-child-summary)
